Translate the following text from Czech: Movement for Civil Rights issued a travel warning for Missouri
National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) issued a warning to people of color traveling to Missouri based on state discriminatory laws and racist attacks.

The NAACP travel advisory for the state of Missouri, effective August 28, 2017, urges African American travelers, visitors, and residents of Missouri to exercise heightened vigilance while traveling across the state due to a series of racially motivated incidents currently occurring throughout the state.

The NAACP stated that it took this step based on current Missouri state laws that make it difficult to prosecute racially motivated crimes in court, as well as the result of negotiations by agencies involved in the criminal proceedings which disproportionately target minorities.
There is a violation of civil rights.
People are stopped by police just because of the color of their skin, they're attacked or killed, said NAACP president for Missouri Rod Chapel to the Kansas City Star.
The complaints are mounting in large numbers.
It is the first warning of its kind that an organization has issued for the state of the United States.
Among the incidents cited by the organization were racist slurs directed at black students at the University of Missouri and the death of Tory Sanders, a black man from Tennessee.

He died under disputed circumstances at the beginning of this year after an accident occurred while traveling across the state, when fuel ran out and he was arrested by police without any charges for committing a crime.
The travel advisory also highlights a recent statement from the highest state's attorney in Missouri, which states that drivers of black skin have a 75% higher chance of being stopped by police.
The purpose of travel advisories is to warn people and their families, friends, and colleagues about potential risks in Missouri, said Chapel.
People must be prepared - they should bring money with them for any potential deposit or notify their relatives that they are planning to travel the state.
According to the latest numbers from the FBI's program, there were over 800 reported cases of hate crimes in Missouri in 2015, placing the state 16th among all states.
Travel warning is also a response to the new Missouri law that makes it easier to sue a company for discrimination in providing accommodation or employment.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) issued travel advisories for Texas and Arizona after the states approved an immigration law that allows state officials to detain people based on violating this law, which the ACLU claims will improve racial profiling.

Travel recommendations are usually issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for foreign countries, but in recent times, law firms have resorted to these measures as a response to specific laws and trends within the US.

Sally Anne Bowman was murdered.
The girl from Croydon was murdered by chef Mark Dixie directly in the restaurant where she worked in 2005, stabbing her with a sharp knife.
The victim and the killer had planned to have sex and smoke marijuana before he killed her.
The killer sat in a nearby café and watched with great interest as the meticulous detective examined the crime scene.
